utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in court today. Madam Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-83-T, the Prosecutor versus Rasim Delic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could we have the appearances, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours, Counsel, and everyone in and around the courtroom. Daryl Mundis and Aditya Menon for the Prosecution, assisted by our case manager, Alma Imamovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to the colleagues from the OTP, to everyone in and around the courtroom. Vasvija Vidovic and Nicholas Robson for the Defence of General Rasim Delic, with legal assistant Lejla Gluhic, and also assisted by our intern, Ms. Tineke Baird.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I guess we haven't got any housekeeping. We'll just go straight into calling the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, prior to calling our witness, we will deliver a brief opening statement, then we will move on to our witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: By all means. I thought you were jumping that part. Thank you very much, Madam Vidovic. Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I will be delivering the opening statement this morning. Before I start, if at this stage, I could hand up some documents to the Court and also to my learned friends on the other side. What you'll find is this is a one-page outline of the points that I will be raising during the opening statement. I can also tell Your Honours that during the course of the opening statement, the Defence will be showing some slides which set out quotations from documents and judgements to which I will be referring during the course of the opening statement. Your Honours, you now have the documents. I anticipate that my opening statement will take about one hour, and I'll begin. It can be said that a criminal trial is like a journey. Last July, all the parties in this courtroom, the Judges, the Prosecution, and the Defence, started off on a journey to ascertain the guilt or innocence of General Rasim Delic. It's been a long journey, but you'll be pleased to note that we are over the halfway stage in that journey. In many ways, it's been a remarkable journey, with the Trial Chamber travelling to Sarajevo on two occasions to hear witnesses. As with all long journeys, it is useful to take stock of the situation and see where we have come from, where we have reached, and where we will be going. Your Honours, that is what I intend to do this morning. Before I do so, however, I'd like to say a few words about the burden and standard of proof. The Prosecution brings this case. It prepared the indictment, it decided how to plead the case, and it decided which facts it would rely upon to prove its case. In bringing its case, the burden of proof falls squarely on the Prosecution at all times to prove the guilt of General Delic. The Defence does not have to prove anything. This presumption of innocence applies at all stages of the case, including, of course, the Defence case. In order to convict General Delic of any of the charges that he faces, you must be certain or sure of guilt. The evidence must be clear and unequivocal, and nothing less will suffice. Finally, the criminal standard of proof beyond reasonable doubt applies to each element of the alleged crimes. It also applies to each important fact which forms a necessary step on the way to conviction. Turning, then, Your Honours, to the first part of the opening, where we've come from; and during this part, I'd like to look back over aspects of the Prosecution case and make some comments. I'd also like to highlight some issues of importance for the Defence. The first point to make is that in bringing its case, the Prosecution has chosen to tell a simple story. You can understand why. Simple stories are often the best. However, in doing so, the Prosecution has dealt with matters superficially and it has failed to dig down into the detail of the case. With regard to the background to this case, you can understand why they would wish to avoid the detail, because it is a grave and complex story. It begins with the disintegration of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, which led to the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina declaring independence in March of 1992. Already, at that time, attacks and ethnic cleansing had commenced on Bosnian territory at the hands of Bosnian Serbs acting together with the JNA. Immediately, the Bosnian leadership was faced with the massive task of creating an army from scratch in order to defend its people. We've heard how the state lacked almost every basic requirement in that regard. It had no conscription system, it had no way to assess what manpower was available, there were no weapons to arm soldiers, and in stark contrast to the Serbs, it had virtually no heavy weapons such as tanks and artillery. The result of the United Nations' arms embargo imposed in 1991 meant that there was no way to rectify this serious imbalance. There was a dearth of uniforms, weapons, and fuel, and we know that the particular problem was the lack of trained and experienced officers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I have a problem. You're telling us of the status of the Army of Bosnia like you are arguing a closing argument. You're not telling us what you're going to be doing. Are you suggesting that what you are telling us is fact; and if it is fact, have you led evidence to give us those facts?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am highlighting the evidence that we've heard, and I'm touching upon salient issues for the Defence case. We will hear further evidence that touches upon these issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, but do we need to rehash the evidence that we have heard at this stage? That's precisely my problem. I would have imagined that an opening statement is going to tell us what you intend to show us, not what the Prosecution has done, because we have all heard that and you'll summarise that in your closing argument anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's not my proposal to summarise the state of evidence at this stage. What I'd like to do is highlight some issues of importance for the Defence. I'll move on from the background and touch upon more salient, or what you may think are more salient, issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next matter, and we say that this is another omission in the Prosecution case, relates to the army itself. In telling its simple story, the Prosecution has, to a large extent, ignored the reality of what an army is and what an army does. By its nature, an army is a highly-complex organisation, composed from huge numbers of men. In the Bosnian Army, there were over 200.000 soldiers. As to its structure, an army is a hierarchy. It is composed of different interconnected levels that each work in concert towards meeting the ultimate mission of the army, and that mission is set by the political leadership. At each level, it has to be absolutely clear who is in charge. If it's not clear who is giving the orders at each level and the orders aren't followed, then, in the chaos of warfare, there is absolutely no hope of having a controlled army. In --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may ask a question: If we don't have a controlled army, why do we go to war at all? Isn't it so that if we don't have a controlled army, then we shouldn't go to war, if control of the army is such a strict condition, senior corps or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to move to issues of command and control and highlight these; and perhaps, through my opening statement, I'll be able to elaborate on this very --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My problem is I can't resist asking these questions, because you sounded like you're giving us a closing argument. You're giving us an analysis and criticising the case of the Prosecution. You are not telling us what the Defence intends to do. I really don't know what you are doing, Mr. Robson, with due respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: We have heard an amount of evidence during the Prosecution case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I know what we have heard. My --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I know what we have heard. My question is: Is this the time to analyse what we have heard or is this the time to get a road map of where the Defence wants to take us?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you'll allow me, I will expand upon this point and you'll see, I hope, where we are going.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I hope we can.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: In the indictment and in pleading the case, and here I refer to paragraph 15 of the indictment, the Prosecution would suggest that General Delic, as Main Staff commander, planned every combat operation and controlled every man. He would have you believe that he had effective communications across the various zones of responsibility in which the Bosnian Army operated. However, Your Honours, we will be asking you to dig beneath the surface of this superficial approach and look to what is the reality of command; and in this respect, you will be hearing evidence. You will be hearing that in an army, you will find different levels of command. In the words of General Sir Rupert Smith, who was the UNPROFOR commander in Bosnia in 1995, he said the following: "Wars and conflicts are conducted at four levels; political, strategic, operational, and tactical, with each level sitting within the context of the order, in descending order from political." The first, political level, is the source of power and decision. In modern conflict, it is the political leadership that controls the military, and it is there that the purpose of entering into the conflict is decided. Your Honours, during the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the political level consisted of the Presidency, which was the highest civilian political body. It sat as Supreme Command, and President Alija Izetbegovic held the position as head of the army and that was in his capacity as supreme commander. Moving down to the next level, the strategic, this is the level where the political decisions to use military force are translated into military directions, and what Rupert Smith said about this is that: "It must never be forgotten that the political considerations provide the context within which the strategy rests. Therefore, the relationship between the political and strategic levels must always be very close." Your Honours, this level involves devising strategic plans to meet the goals fixed at the political level. The strategy sets the mission of the army, and it was at the strategic level that General Delic functioned. At the next level down, we have the operational, and here what Rupert Smith said was: "The operational commander must make his plan, his campaign, which designates the path towards his final objective, given to him by the strategic commander, and orchestrates the activities of his Command to achieve tactical objectives that take the Command, as a whole, in the designated direction." And, Your Honours, at the operational level, and this is what you'll be hearing, we have the units of the corps and the division. In making plans to meet the objectives given by the strategic commander, a corps commander will have a good deal of autonomy. It is at this level that the decisions will be made about the units to be deployed, and combat actions will be drawn up. It was at this level that we found the commanders of the 2nd and 3rd Corps and also the division commanders. And then, Your Honours, finally, we have the tactical level, and it is at this level at which battles, fights, and engagements actually take place. This level is about the movement and use of military force, and this level concerns the units below the division level. In the Bosnian Army, those were the brigades, battalions, companies, and platoons. And, so, by understanding the levels of command, we can see that General Delic played a role at the political level through his attendance at Presidency sessions from time to time, but more importantly the evidence in this case shows that he worked at the strategic level, where he devised strategic plans and issued strategic directives such as the annual directive. Only by understanding these concepts can you fully understand General Delic's role during the war. It shows the types of decisions he made and also the type and nature of information that he needed to have available to him. Your Honours, in connection with this, we should also consider the chain of command; and in this case, the Prosecution must show that there was a chain of command linking everyone from the highest level to the lowest. Concerning proof of a superior subordinate relationship, the Appeals Chamber held in the Halilovic appeal that the ability to exercise effective control, in the sense of a material power to prevent or punish, necessitates a pre-existing relationship of subordination, hierarchy, or chain of command. So, Your Honours, it follows that the Prosecution must prove that a chain of command existed. Furthermore, it must show exactly what the chain of command was, from General Delic at the top, all the way down to his alleged subordinate, the Mujahedin fighter at the bottom, and that is the person who is alleged to have committed the crime. Unless it's a case where it's suggested that the senior commander had a direct link to the foot soldiers many levels below him, which certainly has not been pleaded in this case, the Prosecution must show effective control at each level of the chain of command, and this is something I'd like you to bear in mind during the course of the Defence case. Your Honours, this would entail showing, first, that General Delic was in effective control of the corps commands; next, that the corps commander was in effective control of the division commander; then, the division commander was in effective control of the El Mujahedin commander, whoever that may be; then, the El Mujahedin commander was in effective control of any interim commander within the El Mujahedin organisation; then, finally, that interim commander, if any, was in effective control of the perpetrators of the alleged crimes. Your Honours, in considering this chain of command, we'd also say that it's important for you to consider the role played by IKM Kakanj, Command Post Kakanj, which was the Supreme Command Staff's command post in the field. We'll be hearing more about this and the role that they played. Moving on to my next point, Your Honours, and this is General Delic's right to delegate, this is something that hasn't been explored during the Prosecution case, and we think it's a very important issue. As Main Staff commander, General Delic clearly held an important position, but you have to remember he was not omnipotent. He could not be expected to do the impossible. In meeting his duties as Main Staff commander, General Delic had the right to delegate responsibilities to his subordinates. Indeed, the army would have ground to a halt had he not had the ability to pass on tasks for his subordinates to carry out. When he became aware of problems relating to command and control, General Delic was entitled to issue orders to his subordinates through the chain of command to resolve those problems. He was not required to resolve the problem himself. In giving such instructions, he didn't have to give detailed orders. Also, having issued such orders, unless it was brought to his attention that the instructions could not be carried out, he was entitled to assume that they had been acted upon and the problem had been fixed. Similarly, when allegations of criminal acts were brought to his attention, he was entitled to, and, indeed, he was expected to, delegate their investigation to others through the chain of command. He had no duty to oversee the investigation himself. In the High Command case, it was held that a modern war, such as the last war, entails a large measure of decentralisation. A high commander cannot keep completely informed of the details of military operations of subordinates and, most assuredly, not of every administrative measure. He has the right to assume that details entrusted to responsible subordinates will be legally executed. The President of the United States is the Commander in Chief of its military forces. Criminal acts committed by those forces cannot, in themselves, be charged to him on the theory of subordination. The same is true of other high commanders in the chain of command. Criminality does not attach to every individual in this chain of command. From that fact alone, there must be personal dereliction. And, Your Honours, during the Defence case, we will be looking at the responsibility that was attributed to the Military Security Service for investigating and taking measures against army members suspected of committing crimes. And, Your Honours, in this regard, we will show that the duty of the Military Security Service accorded with the findings of the Appeals Chamber in the Halilovic appeal, and in that case where it was held: "According to the applicable ABiH rules, reflected in the findings of the Trial Chamber, it was the Military Security Service or SVB which had to 'take the reasonable measures to find the perpetrator of the criminal offence' when there was a 'reasonable suspicion that a criminal offence triable by military courts had been committed.'" Your Honours, turning to my next point, this concerns the way the Prosecution has sought to define the Mujahedin. And I take on board that now is not the time for closing speeches, but I would like to make some points. The Defence takes the position that in its pleadings that the Prosecution has prepared, the indictment is confused. There are problems with the way that the Prosecution characterizes the foreign fighters that came to Bosnia. Initially, the Prosecution portrays all foreign fighters as one cohesive, homogenous group. This is paragraph 12 in the indictment. In that paragraph, it refers to Mujahedin or Holy Warriors beginning to arrive in Bosnia-Herzegovina sometime during the middle of 1992. It then refers to the Mujahedin as a collective entity and asserts that they were prepared to conduct a Dzihad or Holy War. Next, in paragraph 13 of the indictment, it alleges that at some stage, after the 19th of November, 1992, the Mujahedin was incorporated into and subordinated into the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade and other units of the 3rd Corps. This, Your Honours, it appears the Prosecution is suggesting that this collective entity became integrated into 3rd Corps units. And then, finally, in paragraph 24 of the indictment, which deals with the events at Maline on the 8th of June, 1993, it talks of an attack which included the 306th Mountain Brigade, the 7th Muslim Brigade, and the Mujahedin. So, Your Honours, it appears we've gone full circle and the Mujahedin has, once again, been pleaded as a collective unit. Your Honours, what is the Prosecution saying? It is confusing, and perhaps the reason for that is because the Prosecution wishes to ignore the reality of the situation. The evidence revealed so far, and the evidence that you will hear more of, shows that there were numerous groups of Mujahedin fighters. Many of the groups were based in Central Bosnia and some were located very close to each other. They were distinct and independent groups and had different goals. It would be wrong to consider that the Mujahedin was one united, single group. Your Honours, turning to the events in Bikosi, and, again, just highlighting an important issue for the Defence, we do not dispute that 24 persons were killed there. It is, however, the Defence position that the Prosecution will have serious problems either proving the identity of the perpetrators or showing that they were members of an identifiable group. We would remind you that then the Prosecution has to prove that a superior-subordinate relationship, through a chain of command, existed between General Delic and the perpetrators. And, finally, in this regard, a further crucial issue for the Trial Chamber to determine is whether General Delic had assumed command of the Bosnian Army at the time the crimes were committed. The issue of assumption of command is something that will be explored in the Defence case. Turning to the alleged crimes in 1995 and the alleged effective control over the El Mujahedin Detachment, in the event that the Chamber finds the crimes were committed, and the Defence takes the position that the crime-base evidence is extremely confusing, particularly with regard to September 1995, the Prosecution will, once again, need to identify the perpetrators of the crimes or at least show which group of Mujahedin, if any, they belonged to. As to whether General Delic exercised effective control over the El Mujahedin Detachment at the time that the alleged crimes were committed, the Appeals Chamber has emphasised the need for a Trial Chamber to look for indicators of control. In the Blaskic appeal, the Appeals Chamber reviewed the evidence and specified a range of factors that could constitute indicators of effective control. We'd like to you have these indicators of effective control in your mind during the course of the Defence case. Those factors that the Appeals Chamber spoke of included the following: Number 1, evidence that the accused was not only able to issue orders, but that those orders were actually followed; 2, evidence that the alleged subordinates were not under the control of the armed force to which they allegedly belonged and that they acted towards their own criminal agenda; 3, evidence showing the alleged subordinates enjoyed the protection of and acted on the orders of others; 4, evidence showing that they were not de facto commanded by the accused; 5, evidence that the unit was attached to a different chain of command than that of the accused; 6, evidence that the unit only accepted the authority of another person; 7, evidence that the unit did not have any obligations towards the accused, and, finally, number 8, evidence concerning any person or entity that a unit reports to. So, Your Honours, it follows that those indicators can, and we say should, be taken into account by the Trial Chamber in assessing whether effective control existed. Your Honours, I was going to highlight a few extracts from the evidence that we've heard pertaining to effective control of the Mujahedin, but I think I'll move on, in light of Your Honour's earlier indication. But what I would say is, and this is important when considering the Defence case, when a military unit, in this case the El Mudjahedin Detachment, takes its own decision whether to participate or not in an action, that is not military control. A unit has to be dependable. When there is a process of negotiations and discussion, where an order to carry out action is only issued when the unit has given approval to participate, that is not military control. In due course, the Chamber will have to weigh and evaluate all the indicators of effective control. The Defence position is that the Prosecution has serious problems. Your Honours, I'll turn briefly to the issue of knowledge, and this is the issue of whether General Delic knew or had reason to know that the crimes had or were about to be committed. I'm not going to be reviewing the evidence, but what I'd like to highlight is: Considering the "had reason to know" standard, it is for the Prosecution to show that the accused had in his possession such information which would have put him on notice of offences committed by subordinates. That was in the Celubici appeal judgement, and, Your Honours, that is a very high standard. The Appeals Chamber subsequently came to consider the "had reason to know" standard during the Krnojelac appeal; and in that case, the Appeals Chamber made it clear that where the Prosecution is relying upon knowledge that subordinates have committed prior offences in order to prove or provide sufficiently-alarming information that would put a commander on notice, the commander must have notice of the same type of crime. In that case, notice that subordinates were conducting acts amounting to cruel treatment in the form of beatings was not sufficient to give the accused notice that they had or were about to commit torture. And, Your Honours, this legal holding is of critical importance in this case. We have heard evidence that an amount of information was available to various parts of the Bosnian Army, which suggested that a minority of the El Mudjahedin Detachment were involved in a degree of wrongdoing. If the Prosecution wishes to rely on information relating to prior wrongdoing, then in line with the Krnojelac appeal judgement, it will have to show that the information concerned the same type of crimes as those alleged in the indictment. And, Your Honours, our position is that it will have serious problems in this regard. Additionally, it will have to show that such information was in the possession of General Delic. Your Honours, I'll move along briefly or quickly and come to the second part, and this is where we've reached. I know that you don't want to hear a closing speech, and I will deal with this simply. The Defence position is that there are problems with the crime-base evidence, and there are no indicators of effective control. Our position is that the case should fall at this point in time, as the Prosecution cannot prove its case beyond reasonable doubt, and that is before we even come to the issue of knowledge. We believe that if we stop the case right now, on the evidence before the Chamber, General Delic would be acquitted. However, we acknowledge that we would be taking a big risk by not deciding to call evidence. Also, in the light of the Prosecution's, in what we would say, rather simplistic approach, we recognise there are certain issues in respect to which the Chamber might benefit from further evidence, and that brings me to the final part of this opening statement, and that is where we're going. We hope to bring a focused case dealing with specific issues. We will call further evidence to show that following the arrival of the foreign Mujahedin fighters, they did not become a unified, single group. We will show that they were different and unrelated groups that acted independently of each other. Our evidence will show that at the time of the crimes committed in Bikosi, not one of these groups was under the effective control of General Delic. Further, we'll show that these groups were not part of the 7th Muslim Brigade or the 306th Mountain Brigade and that they didn't act together with them. We'll confirm that the 7th Muslim Brigade did not take part in the events of the 8th of June, 1993. As to General Delic, we will show that he did not receive information concerning the events on the 8th of June. We will shed light on the circumstances in which he found himself at the end of June and in early July 1993. At that time, there was a threat that Sarajevo would fall due to a coordinated attack by Croat and Serb forces; and, furthermore, there was a threat of an armed uprising by rogue units of the 1st Corps which attacked the Main Staff and also attacked police stations in Sarajevo. This was at the very time that General Delic was supposed to have received information concerning the events in Maline. We will shed light on the divisions which existed in the Main Staff at that point in time, divisions which were caused by the change in command. You'll see that this had a major effect on the functioning of the Main Staff, particularly its Operative Centre, and that had a direct impact on the flow of information to the Supreme Command Staff. Next, we'll show that General Delic did everything within his powers to implement the decision of the president and also the will of the International Community to place the foreign Mujahedin fighters under control. In that respect, we will show the decision to form the El Mudjahedin Detachment was motivated by a desire to place them within the command-and-control system. We will show that General Delic will not receive any reports relating to the detachment about criminal behaviour which demonstrated that they had a propensity to mistreat or harm prisoners of war during combat. Concerning the El Mudjahedin Detachment, we will lead further evidence to demonstrate their total independence from the army and their sophisticated ability to bring men, weapons, and money into the country. We will call evidence about the problems relating to the formation of the El Mudjahedin Detachment and show that the unit was not established correctly and lacked proper records. We will show that there were rules which regulated the membership of foreigners in the Bosnian Army which were disregarded by the detachment. We will also hear about rules which were used to allocate premises to the El Mudjahedin Detachment. Your Honours, we will show clearly that General Delic did not have overall authority and responsibility for the functioning of the army, as the Prosecution claims in the indictment. Nor was he responsible for the planning and directing of all army operations. We will examine and clarify the role of Command Post Kakanj in the system of command and control and, in particular, its role in conveying information to General Delic. You will also hear about General Delic's preoccupations during the summer and autumn of 1995. That role involved coordinating joint operations with the Croatian HV, dealing with UNPROFOR and NATO, and also drumming up support from allied countries. You will hear about the steps that General Delic took, as a responsible commander, to introduce a functioning command-and-control system within the army and his steps to ensure that international humanitarian law was respected. In this connection, Your Honours, we will lead further evidence to show that General Delic, again as a responsible commander, took significant steps to train his men and professionalise the army. Your Honours, we'll hear from a military expert. He is someone who will come and speak about military authority and the factors that indicate whether there is command and control. He will examine the situations which can lead to a breakdown of control. He will explain the different levels of command that I've already mentioned today; political, strategic, operational, and tactical, and he will elaborate on how each level affects the commander's role and duty. As to the events in September 1995 in the Ozren-Vozuca region, we will show that General Delic did not plan or command Operation Farz. We will show that he didn't decide upon the participation of the El Mudjahedin Detachment in the combat activities. We will also show that for the earlier combat action in July, again General Delic did not order those actions or command them. With regard to the El Mudjahedin Detachment, Your Honours, we will show that long before the combat activities in Vozuca, General Delic acted properly in issuing orders concerning the treatment of the detachment. He approved the plan for operative actions Vranduk and Trebevic 3 and 4, and he acted as responsible commander in taking steps for problems that were brought to his attention. And then finally, Your Honours, we will shed light on the role that General Delic made in the establishment of lasting peace in Bosnia and Herzegovina and also evidence of his character. And, so, Your Honours, that concludes the opening statement. I note the time. Would it be your intention that we call the first witness now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed. Thank you very much, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, is it possible perhaps to go on a break right now, because we were not able to make an exact estimate of how long this would take, so the witness will actually be here at 10.30, according to the information that we have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you then suggesting that we take a break up to 10.30?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, if possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic, do we know where the witness is at the moment?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not sure, Your Honour. Perhaps we could move into private session right now so that I can explain something, if you allow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are in the open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I guess, by the change of seats, I call on you, Madam Vidovic. Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You do want to be in open session?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Madam Vidovic. May the witness please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, and good morning to you, sir. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Hubo -- pardon, Mr. Ribo. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: As you know, I will be examining you today on behalf of the Defence for Mr. Rasim Delic. Let me just ask you, before I start putting questions to you, to make a small pause before answering my questions so that we avoid overlapping. We speak the same language, and it is important that everything we say is reflected in the transcript. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: Yes, fully.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ribo, can you tell us when and where you were born? Can you give us your full name?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: My name is Ribo, father's name Ibrahim. My name is Haso. I was born on the 25th of February, 1956, in the village of Kljaci, Travnik Municipality, Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic, I got it as 1965 in the summary that I was given. Are we on the same page or is it 1956?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if we wrote "1965," then my apologies. The year is 1956.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ribo, what is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: I'm a Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Which schools have you completed?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: After completing a civilian high school, I graduated from the Military Academy for Land Forces, the Department of Armoured Units, in Belgrade and Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Where did you serve before the war?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: Before the war, I served in Zajecar for a number of years; and for a shorter period of time, I spent in Jastrebarsko and in the Tuzla garrison.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you hold a rank in the former JNA?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: Yes. I held the rank of captain first class.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us where you lived before the war?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: Before the war, my family and I lived in Zajecar. Shortly before the war, on the 25th of February, 1992, we moved to Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: What were your duties at the start of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: Shortly after my arrival in Travnik, I reported to the Staff of the Territorial Defence, because the decision of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina had been issued to the effect that the only legitimate armed force in Bosnia-Herzegovina was the Territorial Defence, and that was when I joined the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This decision by the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina concerning the armed forces, was it accepted by all the citizens in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: Of course, it was not. It was not accepted by the Croat people, because the Croatian Democratic Community of Bosnia-Herzegovina passed a decision setting up their own armed forces under the name of "Croatian Defence Council."

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did all the Muslims of Central Bosnia accept the Territorial Defence as their own army?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: Of course, they did not, either, especially so the Patriotic League, which had a special view in that regard, as well as the Green Berets, which were the first ones to put up resistance and did not accept the Territorial Defence as their own armed force.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please explain to us, why was there a resistance to accepting the Territorial Defence by the Democratic League and the Green Berets?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: They resisted the idea because they did not have full confidence or trust in the Travnik Municipal Staff of the Territorial Defence, because they believed that this was a structure belonging to the former Yugoslavia and that the Territorial Defence was a socialist creation composed of the so-called "Reds"; the communists, that is.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Save for the members of the Green Berets and the Patriotic League, were there others who resisted the setting up of the Territorial Defence among the Muslim population?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: Of course, there were. As I've just said, the Territorial Defence was considered to be a socialist structure. Resistance was to be found also among the Muslim religious community -- communities.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And why was that, Mr. Ribo?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: Due to the very structure of the Command of the TO Staff, and also due to the fact that they saw a purely ethnic army being formed, such as the HVO, such as the HOS, they decided to set up their own purely Muslim army that would represent and be responsible only to the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before I move on to documents, let me ask you this: Do you recall when it was that you became the head of the Travnik TO Municipal Staff?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: I believe it was in the month of June.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Which year was that?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: 1992. Before that, in early April, or rather, in late April, I became a member of the TO Staff and was appointed the head of the TO Staff for Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness be shown D902. Can you please scroll the document down so that we can see the signature. That's at page 3 of the English version.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: A moment ago, you said that the religious circles were diffident of the Territorial Defence because of the composition of the staff. While we were waiting for the English version to appear, did you have a chance to look at the Bosnian version? Tell me, please, have you seen the document before?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This is a document by the TO Staff, dated the 26th of June, 1992. Is this your name, and do you know anything about the document, what it refers to?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: Yes. The name and the signature are mine. The document is related to the request by the TO Staff for the region of Zenica, that we should deliver to them a list of the employees that were employed in the Travnik TO Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please pause for a moment. Could we have the English version showing page 1 again, so that Their Honours can follow. Very well. Can we turn to page 2 now, and I'm referring to the English version. Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ribo, we can see a number of names here. They were the individuals making up the Staff, as you said. How many Muslims were among them?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: Out of the 13 employees I had at the time, four were Muslims, four were Serbs, and five were Croats.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Your Honours, can this document be assigned an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document will become Exhibit number 1175.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your TO Staff, throughout its existence, was it equipped with facilities enabling it to work?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: I will be brief. In addition to the physical premises and the employees, we had nothing else. Our material and technical equipment that the TO had purchased, or rather, the people of Travnik and the people of Bosnia-Herzegovina, were at some point seized by the JNA. This was the case for several municipality in BH, and they were stored in a village near Travnik. Some of the equipment was relocated to the Serb-controlled territory and to the JNA-controlled territory. In addition to the ammunition and communications equipment, they also had some food stuffs. Whatever could be taken away to the territory of Republika Srpska was taken there.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: To the best of your recollection, in the course of the summer of 1992, at the time the Staff was in existence, how many men and how many rifles did it have, if you know?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: We analysed our combat readiness, which was quite typical for commands; and in the month of July, we had some 5.100 men and between 1.000 and 1.200 pieces of infantry weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Does this then mean that in the Travnik area, your manpower levels were sufficient or pretty high, but you didn't have enough weapons?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: Precisely so. We did have many men, able-bodied men. Unfortunately, we lacked weapons, and we had to keep the manpower at the levels that they were. We couldn't recruit anymore because we had weapons in short supply.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ribo, under such circumstances, were you in any need of volunteers at all?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: No, not at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The shortage of ammunition and weapons that you described, did it have any bearing on the further developments in terms of the war in the area?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: Of course. The problem persisted throughout the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ribo, can you briefly describe for us the military and humanitarian situation in Travnik as you found it when you got there, or rather, the situation that prevailed in Travnik in 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In connection with this, Your Honours, I should like the witness to look at map D1045 and to mark some locations on the map. Your Honours, while we're waiting for the map to appear, let me ask you this: You will let me know when I should stop my examination for the next break, since we're out of the usual times now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It will be at quarter to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you have a map before you which I want you to use to indicate the line of defence opposite the Serb forces in the Travnik area and the defence line of the Territorial Defence, or rather, of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina opposite the Croat forces, if you have the pointer there. I believe you have the electronic pen in front of you. Do you think we should zoom in on the map?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: Please, if that could be done. As it is now, you can't even make out anything under the microscope.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It has been enlarged, but the area where I should indicate the defence line opposite the Serb forces is not visible at present.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you scroll down a bit, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To the right is Okrinje.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please circle it?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: [Marks] That's above Lukavica, several kilometres above Lukavica, then across Srebreno Hill, which isn't visible on the map, either. It's a bit to the north.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please draw on the map itself and not out of the map. I think you marked it outside of the map.

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: The line of defence, the position of the Serb forces, is outside the range of map.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I understand that, but we will not have it on the map, so I would like you to actually indicate it on the map.

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: [Marks] Srebreno Brdo, Poljice, Crni Vrh, Savo, and Pavo, the television tower at Opaljenik, the road leading towards Opaljenik, then Galica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. These names that the witness is mentioning, can we see them on the map? I'm finding difficulty seeing them.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, when you mention a name, if it's marked on the map, I would kindly ask you to circle it.

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: [Marks] Well, I see very well here Opaljenik, the TV tower, and then nearby -- this is quite a small scale. I know the terrain, but the scale is quite small for me to be able to actually indicate this on the map.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Very well. Just circle the names that are marked on the map?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: [Marks] Galica is here, and then Harambasine Vode.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And Harambasine Vode, is that on the map?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In that case, can you please write that in yourself?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now we would need to move the map to the right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you do that, you are going to lose the markings, Madam Vidovic. Did you hear me? If you move the map to the right, you are going to lose the markings.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. I understand that, Your Honour. For now, yes, that's the problem. Well, let this stay as it is now, the line towards the Serb forces, and now we can ask this to be tendered. Then we can move the map so we can see another part of it, so that the witness can mark the line facing the Croat forces. I would like to have an exhibit number for this particular map, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It will be given an exhibit number. It's admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will become Exhibit number 1176.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes. Now you can move it, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Defence counsel has requested that the map be moved to the right. Are we able to do that?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, can you please look at the map, and can you tell us where we should --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We've got a problem. We've lost that part that the witness had marked earlier. It has not been saved. So can we start all over again, please. I'm sorry about that, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, perhaps we have a solution that will save some time. I could indicate to the witness or I could show to the witness a map, a hard copy, that he marked for me yesterday, then we can look at it on the ELMO, and then he can confirm that this is so. I think that we will save some time if we do it this way, and in future I will try to bring only clean copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before you put it on the ELMO, Mr. Mundis?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If I could just have a look at that, please, before it goes on to the ELMO, I'd be grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the document be shown to Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My only concern is that this was marked out of court, Madam Vidovic, and I'm not doubting your word that it was marked by the witness, but it would have been more probative if the witness was making the markings in court. And while I'm speaking, let me just mention that the Registrar has just advised me that the Exhibit 1176, which we thought we had lost, actually it has been captured. I don't know whether that changes your strategy, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if it's been saved, then I think it's better for the witness to continue marking the document here, indicating the lines of defence; and then if you can just return to us the hard copy of the map, I would like to ask the usher to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Vidovic. Sir, can you give Madam Vidovic that hard copy. Then has the map then been shifted to the right? Okay. The witness may continue now. Thank you very much, Madam Vidovic. I'm sorry for that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It hasn't been moved.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Should it be moved to the left or to the right?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: To the right. I need this part more. [Indicates] Well, it looks as if there's nothing more on this map. From what I can see, the map is what it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It should be the same map which you were marking yesterday. Can you see the lines of defence? It should be the same map.

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: Yes, but the entire territory is not on this map, not -- the entire territory of Travnik is not on this map.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, can you show us what you can see?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: Yes, very well. [Marks] This is it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On this map, can you see the Biljani area?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please mark the Biljani area on the map? Maybe if you have a different colour, you can use that to mark the Biljani area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I just have two very brief points. First of all, I'm not sure if the record, as it exists currently, is going to be of assistance in helping us decipher this map in the future. Perhaps some questions can be asked about that. And I also do want to put on the record that the witness still has the hard copy map in front of him and seems to be consulting that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. But I asked that that hard copy be given back to the Defence counsel. Mr. Registrar or Mr. Court Usher, I asked that the hard copy of that map be given back to the Defence counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ribo, this map, can you see the Biljani area on the map?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: Well, it should be moved for me to be able to see if it's there.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Your Honours, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you just write on the this map that this is the line facing the HVO?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: What I marked is the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now you're asking him to show that. He hasn't told us whether this line is the line facing the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, please, Witness. You heard the question. What you marked, what does that represent?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: This is the line of defence of the Bosnian Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Serbs?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please write that down?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And against whom were these Serb forces fighting at this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Territorial Defence of Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And then can you please indicate "TO Travnik" there?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honours, I don't know if this has been given an exhibit number now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Wait a minute. Before we --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we give it an exhibit number, and before Mr. Mundis speaks, I ask the question and it is stated by the

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then I said: "Against whom were these Serb forces fighting?" The answer was: "The Territorial Defence of Travnik." Is that the correct situation?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the Territorial Defence of Travnik. Okay. Thank you very much. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Again, Your Honours, and I hate to interrupt, but I fear that there will continue to be some confusion later down the road, because it's not clear from this map where these two forces that the witness has testified about were in with respect to the line that's been drawn. I simply want to avoid confusion down the road. He's indicated the Bosnian Serb forces and the TO Travnik forces, but it doesn't appear clear, from the line he's drawn, which force was where on this map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand. I thank my colleague, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please indicate, by arrows, where the Bosnian Serbs were and where the TO Travnik forces were? Just mark that with an arrow.

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: Let me clarify. I can just make two lines, the line of the Bosnian Serbs and the line of the Travnik Municipality TO.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but can you just show us on the map the part where the Bosnian Serbs were and where the TO Travnik was?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: The red line that I marked is the Bosnian Serbs' line.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And on what side were the Bosnian Serbs, Mr. Ribo? That is the question. You know that and we don't know that.

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: Well, perhaps it would be good for me to indicate the defence line, the line where the TO was.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right. You can indicate that.

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: Can we move this?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, you cannot move it.

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: No. Well, I can mark it on the part that I see.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. Can you please do that.

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And now, Mr. Ribo, for purposes of clarification, can you tell us, what does this red line that you marked on this document stand for?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: The red line represents the position of the Serbs in my Travnik front.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And the blue line, what does that represent for purposes of the transcript?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: The blue line represents the positions of the forces of the Travnik Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope that this is now clear and understandable for Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just for the sake of everybody else, if the witness could please write "Travnik Territorial Defence" behind the line which they stood and then "the Bosnian Serbs" behind the line which they stood.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The red one, yes. [Marks]. The Bosnian Serbs were in this area, this direction, the blue.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And can you help us and can you please tell us what this blue circle stands for? Which area is that?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: This is the area of Sesicka Planina, Sesic Mount, and it was isolated like this completely surrounded.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to ask you this, Mr. Ribo: Can you see the Biljanska Valley on this map?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: No. You cannot see it on this part of the map.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Thank you very much. Your Honours, can this map now be given an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: This map has been admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will become Exhibit number 1177.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And can you please tell us which direction we should move the map?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: To the right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Have we captured that?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope that the previous map has been saved. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ribo, can you look at this carefully before you start marking it. Do you see the Biljanska Valley on this map?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you now please circle the Biljanska Valley area?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now, can you explain to us here, can you explain on this map, can you indicate on this map the line held by the Croatian Defence Council in 1992 and 1993? Before that, can you please mark in that this is the Biljanska Valley so that we know.

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: [Marks] Very well. I would need to change the colour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Can you just mark the line of the HVO line of defence and indicate that with arrows.

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: [Marks] Is it possible to enlarge this part of the map?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No. Unfortunately, we can't change anything because we will lose the document.

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: What does -- or what do the blue lines stand for?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: The blue lines stand for the HVO positions in the Biljanska Valley.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please just write "HVO" behind these lines?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: Is this related to the Biljanska Valley only?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, just the Biljani region. To your knowledge, for how long did the lines in the Biljanska Valley stay as they are drawn now?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: Until the conflict broke out with the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you say until the conflict with the HVO broke out, can you tell us what sort of a conflict are you referring to, in terms of time?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: In the spring of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your honour, can this document be given an exhibit number and can the witness be shown a different document. Though, I believe it's time for our break, so perhaps the other document can be dealt with after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: This document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will become Exhibit number 1178.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you very much, Madam Vidovic. I do think we should take a break at this stage. We were supposed to have broken at quarter to. Can we come back at quarter past 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic. And, Madam Vidovic, because of the confusion this morning, we are going to stop at 12.00 so that we go back to our normal time.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I will be mindful of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ribo, let us dwell for some time on the situation in the Travnik area. You've indicated some of the positions and lines of the Serb Army, including the Biljanska Valley, and now I should like to look into the situation in Travnik itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown D1033. For the sake of transcript, before the exhibit appears, this is an excerpt from the book called "Seasons in Hell," by author Ed Vulliamy, that is. Very well. In English, that's page 5. This is the cover page. Can we please turn to page 2 of the Bosnian version. That's the corresponding page. Can you please enlarge a bit the Bosnian version, and I will quote.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, can you have a look, please. Please look at this passage from the book describing the situation in Travnik. I will quote the first sentence and another small part of the text describing Travnik: "If there is a junction in the Bosnian war, a meeting point through which its themes of fear, misery, violence, wit, and courage have passed, it is Travnik, the ancient town in which we awoke dazed the next morning."

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will skip to another passage, to save time, which is somewhere in the middle of the page, starts with, "On the streets ..." in English. In the Bosnian, it's the corresponding.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: "On the streets, there were soldiers everywhere, government army soldiers, Croatian soldiers, black-shirted HOS soldiers. We didn't care who or what they were. This morning, we were on their side. Travnik felt then like some frontier town, a merciful outpost on the edge of territory that had embraced us and taken us in from the madness back out there. "Therefore, the Serbian -- so it was over to Travnik that tens of thousands of deputies were now being herded by the Serbian war machine. With the Croatian border shut, this was the back door. There were 26.000 of them in town already, crammed into gymnasia and schools, all of whom had come along that road." Mr. Ribo, this section of book by Ed Vulliamy, does it describe the situation as it was in Travnik in course of 1992 through to the spring of 1993?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: Relatively speaking, he does portray the situation in Travnik; although, it was far more difficult and complicated, what with the humanitarian crisis, the refugees crisis. It was a total chaos.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honours, can this document be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, we have no objection to the document going into evidence. I do like to place on the record, however, that there have been a number of leading questions this morning. The Prosecution will object when leading questions are asked from this point forward. I would also indicate, so that everyone's on notice, that the Prosecution will be arguing, at the conclusion of the evidence, that leading questions on direct examination, the answers to such questions should be given little or no weight. So I will put that on the record very firmly at this point in time for the benefit of the Defence. I don't like objecting, but I will be doing so when leading questions are put to witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed, it would be very helpful if you would when that happens, because the Bench may not necessarily pick it up when it does happen. This document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number. It is only this page that's being tendered.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will become 1179, Exhibit 1179.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And what is the page number in the book?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Bear with us for a moment, Your Honour. Page 139. I believe we can even see it on our screen somewhere. Your Honours, I will be referring to two more passages from the book, from the same exhibit. Your Honours, the pages --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Can I just take up a matter with you, because I would like to clarify how we apply the rules concerning admission of evidence. This book is clearly not written by an expert. It is an opinion by an author. I don't know if the witness has read the book. The witness had a lot of comments to the parts that we have now admitted; and to be honest, it does seem to me to be a little too nebulous to admit passages from books which the witness has neither read nor written, and which contain only very subjective information to which, on top of it, the witness had had to make several additional comments. So my question is, really: Does this have any probative value at all?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, allow me to explain. Firstly, I referred the witness to the passage of the book describing the situation in Travnik, with which the familiar -- with which the witness is very familiar. As you will see from the next passage that we will be using, the book has partly been written on the basis of the conversations with this witness, and you will see that the author of the book is referring to this very witness. That is the reason why we're using the book; otherwise, I would agree with what you're saying. You will see that there is a direct link between the book and the witness and the conversations that the witness had had with the author of the book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. This is a very helpful addition to what we have previously learned from this page. Am I to understand that the book is the result of a conversation, of an interview with the witness, and that the views expressed in the book are largely ascribed to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely so, Your Honour. This isn't true for the entire book, only for the part dealing with the Travnik area. And my questions will have to do with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In that event, Madam Vidovic, it may have been helpful, and may I suggest that you try and do that in the future, to lay the foundation by saying to this witness: "Are you aware of this book? Do you know who wrote it? Do you know why he wrote it? Do you know who he conducted discussions with before he wrote it? Are you one of those people?" "Yes, I am." Then go on. At least then we have laid the foundation. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I will try to follow that line in the future.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: We were discussing the situation in Travnik in the second half of 1992 and the first half of 1993. You said ...

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we will be referring to two more relevant pages of the document. Perhaps I should have waited for those pages to be shown before asking for an exhibit number. I will come back to you now, Mr. Ribo.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the humanitarian situation. Can you briefly describe the humanitarian situation in Travnik at the time?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: It was more than catastrophic. There was a large number of refugees. I believe that between 80 to 100.000 refugees passed through the area at the time. These were people who were completely lost, who were left without all their property, their dear and near ones. They were psychologically deranged and milling about the town purposelessly. We did our best to provide them with the odd can of food. There was nothing else we could do for them. The situation was so difficult for this small town, situated in a valley, to have to receive such a large number of refugees.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we refer back to the document again, this time page 3 of the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it still D1033?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Then page 1 of the Bosnian version. Please enlarge the text, and please scroll the English version down a bit -- rather, up, scroll up -- or rather, can you scroll down so we can see the last sentence. If Their Honours and the Prosecution could look at the last sentence in the English version, because we will be looking at the text on the following page. Can we now turn to the following page in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ribo, I believe you have managed to read the passage by now. I will quote page 127 of the book, which says: "In recent days, as the commander of the Bosnian Army in Travnik said, 20 refugees had been killed in ambushes by the same egg regulars who had ushered them out onto the road. 'They fire at and shell the people as they come through; and to save themselves, people run off the road into the woods and get lost,' said Commander Haso Ribo." My question is: Is that you that is being referred to?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: Yes. That is my statement that I gave to that journalist who stayed with me in the Staff in Travnik. I practically provided him with accommodation and food, since he had arrived with a refugee convoy from Banja Luka. Then at the point where people are normally taken off the buses, he was taken -- the vehicle, the vehicle was taken away from him. So he had to stay there, and I was kind to him. I provided him with everything he needed, and then I provided him with a vehicle to go to Split.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: What I want to ask you is: Has he, in fact, portrayed accurately your words concerning the situation with regard to refugees or not?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: Yes. He did portray accurately the situation as it was. I went through this with these people. They were going via the Banja Luka-Standard-Vakuf-Vlasic Plateau route, precisely because that route was not inhabited. That's what they were able to do in that part, the Bosnian Serbs. When they were let out from the point where they were disembarked from the buses, that is the last curve on Vlasic towards the Lasva Valley, then they would be firing at those columns, because they had to pass that part on foot until they left Turbe, where they -- they were taken over by us, with our buses, and taken to locations in Travnik, I don't know, in Zenica, and so on. So they simply used artillery fire to shoot at these refugee columns because they did not have their own contact forces in that area and the artillery actions were not risky.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic, just for my own clarification --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was saying that the translation was being done. It's now finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic, at page 46, line 26, you referred us to page 3 of the English version. At page 47, line 11, I heard the interpreter talking of page 127.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, page 3 of the English version is the translation. It's a part of our document, the translation that you have in the exhibit. And page 127 is actually that page in the original book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That clears me. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Can this document please be put away, and I would like to just put one question to you about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: What was the state of mind of those people when they came to Travnik? I'm thinking of the refugees.

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: They were in a very specific --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Calls for speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may respond, Your Honour. I really believe that an average person is able to see and gauge the behaviour and the mental state of a refugee that is coming from this area after shelling and so on, and I don't think in any way that this is an invitation or call for speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic, when you ask for the state of mind, it's a different thing. But if you asked how they looked, it's quite another, and the witness can tell you how they looked to him. He's telling the physical appearance of the people, but a state of mind is something that you and I have no ability to read.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, perhaps it's a question of translation, but I'm going to simplify the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: How did they look?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: They seemed completely lost people. They were just wandering aimlessly about town. Simply, they were not able to control their actions. We had a thousand problems because of that, the command, the civilian authorities in Travnik.
